content: In November 2015, it was noted that an increasing number of women had access to antiretroviral drugs (ARVs) during pregnancy and breastfeeding. This access was aimed at improving maternal health and reducing the risk of mother-to-child transmission of HIV. For instance, in 2012, approximately 75% of HIV-positive pregnant women received ARVs, which was 400,000 more women compared to 2009. This expanded coverage, along with newer ARV regimens, significantly reduced mother-to-child HIV transmission rates. However, in many countries with high HIV prevalence, over half of new pediatric HIV infections occurred during the breastfeeding period. The World Health Organization (WHO), UNAIDS, UNFPA, and UNICEF last revised their guidelines on HIV and infant feeding in 2010. These guidelines, for the first time, recommended the use of ARVs to prevent HIV transmission through breastfeeding. Since then, WHO has updated its recommendations on ARV treatment for HIV-infected adults and children, as well as for the prevention of mother-to-child transmission (PMTCT). However, the public health and programmatic implications of these updates were not fully integrated into infant and young child feeding recommendations in high HIV-prevalence countries. The implementation of global recommendations on HIV and infant feeding at the national level is influenced by several factors. In 2012, UNICEF collected data on the implementation of the 2010 global guidelines to better understand the situation, improve technical assistance, and inform advocacy and resource mobilization. The 2010 guidelines were scheduled for an update in 2015 using the GRADE process outlined by the WHO Guideline Review Committee. To support this, the WHO Department of Maternal, Newborn, Child, and Adolescent Health, in collaboration with UNICEF, evaluated the experiences and challenges related to implementing the 2010 guidelines. This evaluation involved interviews and an online survey targeting three groups: national Ministry of Health representatives, implementing partners, and networks of HIV-infected mothers. The findings summarized progress in 22 UNAIDS priority countries (primarily in sub-Saharan Africa and India) and identified key programmatic questions for the Guideline Development Group to address in the updated guidelines. The evaluation aimed to assess the quality and extent of the implementation of the 2010 global guidelines on HIV and infant feeding in the 22 countries included in the UNAIDS Global Plan. The primary objectives were to collect and analyze information on HIV and infant feeding policies, document challenges in policy implementation, and identify aspects of the 2010 guidelines for potential review. Secondary objectives included assessing progress in implementing recommended interventions, gathering data on capacity-building efforts, and collecting national monitoring and evaluation tools related to infant feeding by HIV-infected mothers. The evaluation used a combination of semi-structured phone interviews and electronic surveys. The interviews targeted national representatives responsible for HIV and infant feeding, while the surveys were directed at implementing partners and organizations involved in HIV-related programs. The survey was available in English and French and designed to take less than 30 minutes to complete. Participants could respond at their convenience over four months, with the option to save and return to the survey. The study population included Ministry of Health representatives, implementing partners, and organizations working on HIV-related programs. The 22 countries included in the evaluation were Angola, Burundi, Botswana, Cameroon, Chad, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Ethiopia, Ghana, India, Ivory Coast, Kenya, Lesotho, Malawi, Mozambique, Namibia, Nigeria, South Africa, Swaziland, Uganda, Tanzania, Zambia, and Zimbabwe. Ethical considerations were addressed by obtaining informed consent from participants before interviews and surveys. The data collected represented the professional views of health workers and did not include personal information. The Ethics Review Committee granted an exemption for the study, as the data focused on professional capacities. The results showed that all 22 countries had at least a protocol or guideline and a training document on HIV and infant feeding. However, none had a stand-alone document dedicated solely to this topic. Most countries recommended breastfeeding with ARV interventions for all HIV-infected mothers, with only two countries adopting an individualized approach based on the mother's condition. Exclusive breastfeeding until six months was recommended in all countries, with variations in recommendations for continued breastfeeding beyond six months. The evaluation highlighted challenges in implementing the guidelines, including resistance from health workers and mothers due to concerns about HIV transmission risks. Some countries reported difficulties in training and resource allocation, while others found implementation relatively easy. Heat treatment of expressed breast milk was included as an option in the guidelines of half the countries, primarily for situations where the mother was temporarily unable to breastfeed. Counseling approaches for HIV-infected mothers varied, with most countries recommending individual or group counseling. However, some countries lacked clear recommendations on what to do if ARVs were unavailable. The evaluation also found that many countries did not plan to update their national documents on HIV and infant feeding unless new international recommendations were issued. Overall, the evaluation provided valuable insights into the progress and challenges of implementing the 2010 global guidelines on HIV and infant feeding. These findings will inform future updates to the guidelines and support efforts to improve maternal and child health outcomes in high HIV-prevalence settings.
